extracted.intended_audience: journalists and reporters covering transgender people and issues
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for journalists on accurate, respectful, and contextual reporting about transgender people, including preferred names/pronouns, terminology, and key issue areas to cover sensitively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the name and pronoun the subject asks you to use
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the name and pronoun the subject asks you to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites the AP Stylebook (2011): reporters should “use the pronoun preferred by the individuals who have acquired the physical characteristics of the opposite sex or present themselves in a way that does not correspond with their sex at birth. If that preference is not expressed, use the pronoun consistent with the way the individuals live publicly.” The New York Times Style Book: “use the name and pronouns (he, his, she, her, hers) preferred by the transgender person.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite a person's transgender status only when pertinent
rubrics_metrics.description: “Cite a person’s transgender status only when its pertinence is clear to the reader.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From NYT Style Book: unless a former name is newsworthy or pertinent, use the name and pronouns preferred by the transgender person. Do not gratuitously identify someone as transgender when it is not relevant to the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: If no pronoun preference is known, follow public presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: If no preference is expressed, use the pronoun consistent with the way the individuals live publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both AP and NYT guidance indicate defaulting to pronouns consistent with how a person lives publicly when the individual's preference isn't known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'transgender' as an adjective, not a noun
rubrics_metrics.description: “Transgender is correctly used as an adjective, not a noun, thus ‘transgender people’ is appropriate but ‘transgenders’ is often viewed as disrespectful.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating transgender identity as a label/noun for people. Use phrasing like 'transgender people' rather than 'transgenders.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'trans' as shorthand when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes 'trans' is common shorthand; be mindful of audience and preference when using abbreviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sensitive to terminology variation across communities
rubrics_metrics.description: “Terminology within the transgender community varies and has changed over time so we recognize the need to be sensitive to usage within particular communities.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn current usage and respect community-specific terms; avoid assuming one term fits all contexts or individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Transgender
rubrics_metrics.description: “A term for people whose gender identity, expression or behavior is different from those typically associated with their assigned sex at birth. Transgender is a broad term and is good for non-transgender people to use.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition to accurately describe who is being discussed; note that it is an umbrella term and that 'trans' is shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Transgender Man
rubrics_metrics.description: “A term for a transgender person who currently identifies as a man.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this term for individuals who identify as men but were assigned a different sex at birth; confirm individual preference where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Transgender Woman
rubrics_metrics.description: “A term for a transgender person who currently identifies as a woman.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this term for individuals who identify as women but were assigned a different sex at birth; confirm individual preference where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Nonbinary
rubrics_metrics.description: “People whose gender is not male or female use many different terms to describe themselves, with nonbinary (sometimes spelled 'non-binary') being one of the most common. Other terms include genderqueer, agender, bigender, and more. None of these terms mean exactly the same thing – but all speak to an experience of gender that is not simply male or female.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the range of nonbinary identities and avoid conflating different terms; ask individuals how they identify and which labels/pronouns they prefer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Gender Identity
rubrics_metrics.description: “An individual’s internal sense of being male, female, or something else. Since gender identity is internal, one’s gender identity is not necessarily visible to others.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that gender identity may not be externally visible and should not be assumed based on appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Transition
rubrics_metrics.description: “The time when a person begins living as the gender with which they identify rather than the gender they were assigned at birth, which often includes changing one’s first name and dressing and grooming differently. Transitioning may or may not also include medical and legal aspects, including taking hormones, having surgery, or changing identity documents (e.g. driver’s license, Social Security record) to reflect one’s gender identity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should note that transitioning is a personal, varied process that may include medical and legal steps; the page also notes medical and legal steps are often difficult to afford—include socioeconomic context when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report violence sensitively and contextually
rubrics_metrics.description: “Transgender people—and transgender women of color specifically—face severe risks for a variety of types of violence, including intimate partner violence, violence fueled by transphobic and homophobic hatred, and violence from law enforcement and corrections officials.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For accurate and sensitive reporting on homicide and other violence, the page recommends reading GLAAD’s 'More Than A Number: Shifting the Media Narrative on Transgender Homicides.' Avoid sensationalizing and provide context about risk patterns and systemic drivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document healthcare access barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: “Transgender people often lack access to basic, comprehensive healthcare. Many medical providers do not provide sex-specific care for transgender patients, or outright deny all care to people who disclose their gender identity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering health issues, highlight access barriers, denial of care, and systemic problems rather than treating care as an individual failing; use authoritative sources for medical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain identification records challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: “A patchwork of state and local laws make it difficult for transgender people to update drivers licenses, birth certificates and other identification records with accurate name and gender markers. The inability to update these records makes it difficult for transgender people to secure bank accounts, attend school, or get a job and make people vulnerable to discrimination and violence in everyday life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe legal/administrative barriers and concrete consequences for everyday life; use state-by-state context when relevant (Movement Advancement Project and state reports cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover employment discrimination and economic vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: “Anti-transgender bias often plays a subtle role in recruiting, hiring, training, and promoting transgender employees. Transgender people experience twice the rate of unemployment as the general population. Transgender people often have trouble even getting minimum wage, entry level jobs, and are forced into criminalized activities to survive.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include data on unemployment and structural barriers, and avoid portraying economic hardship as solely individual fault; seek sources that document workplace discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report criminal justice bias and its effects
rubrics_metrics.description: “Transgender people face routine bias from law enforcement and correctional authorities, ranging from profiling and harassment to abuse and assault. This fosters an environment of mistrust between transgender people and law enforcement, leaving many transgender people with no where to turn when they are at risk or actively facing violence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering interactions with police or the justice system, investigate patterns of mistreatment, institutional policies, and the consequences for community safety and trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult authoritative resources and research
rubrics_metrics.description: Key resources listed include: National Center for Transgender Equality (US Transgender Survey), American Psychiatric Association materials on gender identity/expression, Harvard Kennedy School research on hormones and surgery for transgender youth, Movement Advancement Project state-by-state legal landscape, and GLAAD reporting guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these organizations and reports as reliable background and data sources when reporting on transgender topics; cite relevant studies (e.g., US Transgender Survey) and expert analyses to provide evidence and context.
